title: Foundations
description: You don't need more grammar tables. You need to understand the machine you're operating: input goes in, output comes out, feedback corrects the loop. Learners who understand this loop improve faster than those who memorize rules.

lessons.title: The input → output cycle (in plain words)

steps.body: You don't need more grammar tables. You need to understand the *machine* you're operating: input goes in, output comes out, feedback corrects the loop. Learners who understand this stop wasting months on the wrong activities (like re-reading grammar rules) and start doing the few things that compound. This module is short — it's the operating manual for everything after it.

Think of learning English like learning cricket. Watching matches (input) teaches you what good batting looks like. But you only learn to bat by batting (output) — and by a coach telling you your elbow is wrong (feedback).

- **Input:** listening and reading slightly above your level. This is where your brain *acquires* patterns unconsciously. Rule: lots of it, narrow (one topic at a time), every day.
- **Output:** speaking and writing. This forces your brain to go from "I get the idea" to "I can build the sentence." This is where gaps get *noticed* — you feel the sentence break, and that feeling is learning.
- **Feedback:** correction that is immediate and specific. A coach who says "wrong" helps a little. A coach who says "you dropped the article — it's *an* Etsy account, not *a n*" fixes the error permanently.

steps.heading: Roman Urdu version
steps.body: *Input matlab angrezi andar — sunna, parhna. Output matlab angrezi bahar — bolna, likhna. Sirf andar karne se samajh aayegi, bolna nahi aayega. Sirf bahar karne se ghaltiyan pakki ho jayengi. Dono chahiye, roz.*

steps.heading: What this means for your routine
steps.body: that's why the Daily Routine has all four blocks. Input without speaking = you understand clients but freeze when replying. Speaking without input = you get fluent at your own mistakes.

lessons.title: The consistency design (built for your 2–3 day pattern)

steps.body: Here's the truth: motivation is weather. Systems are climate. Your pattern — strong for 2–3 days, then fading — is normal, not a character flaw. The course is designed around it:

1. **The 20-minute minimum.** On dead days, do 10 min shadowing + 10 min speaking. A short day keeps the chain of *identity* ("I'm someone who practices daily") even when the chain of hours breaks.
2. **Re-entry, not restart.** Missed 5 days? Don't redo Week 1. Open the module you left, read its re-entry note, do one minimum day. Restarting from zero is how courses die.
3. **Same time, same place.** Habit research is boring and unanimous: anchor the routine to an existing habit (after Fajr, after dinner). "I'll do it when I have time" = never.
4. **Make the start stupidly small.** Open Anki. That's it. Starting is the hard part; continuing is easy.

steps.title: Explain the cycle to a friend
steps.prompt: Explain input → output → feedback in 4–6 sentences to a friend (in Roman Urdu if needed, then in English). If you can't explain it simply, re-read Lesson 1.1. Teaching is the fastest test of understanding.
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

lessons.title: The error log method (your most valuable document)

steps.body:
Buy a notebook or open a doc. Title: **My Error Log**. Every time you (or your AI tutor) catch an error in YOUR speech or writing, log it in this format:

Rules of the log:

- **Log only YOUR errors**, not textbook exercises. Your errors are the curriculum.
- **The 5-strike rule:** any error that appears 5 times gets a full drill week (Module 2 has drills for each type). This is how you prevent *fossilization* — errors that feel "good enough" and freeze permanently.
- **Review the log every Sunday** (5 minutes). Read your old errors aloud, correctly. Watching the list shrink is your real progress bar.
steps.example: Date: 3 Oct | My sentence: I was working pastly in 2021 2024 | Fixed: I worked as a sales supervisor from 2021 to 2024 | Rule: finished past time → simple past; "pastly" isn't a word; use "from X to Y" | Count: 3rd time

steps.body:
Every Sunday — or whatever your rest day is — spend 15 minutes on this. Not an hour. Fifteen minutes.

1. **Error log skim (5 min):** Read the week's entries aloud, correctly. Star any error that appeared 3+ times — that's next week's accuracy sprint target.
2. **Recording compare (5 min):** Play 60 seconds of this week's recording against last week's. Write one line: "better at ___, still weak at ___."
3. **Week score (5 min):** Score your Daily Routine adherence, not your English: how many days did you hit the 20-minute minimum? 6–7 = strong. 4–5 = fine. Under 4 = shrink the routine (do the 20-min minimum as the full routine for a week) instead of quitting.
Write the 3 lines in your log. That's the whole review. Small, honest, repeatable — the opposite of the "new month, new me" restart cycle.

steps.prompt:
**Write your re-entry contract**

Finish these sentences honestly, in writing:

1. When I miss 3 days, the thought that stops me from returning is...
2. My 20-minute minimum will happen at (time) in (place)...
3. The person I can tell about this course for accountability is...
4. If I feel "this isn't working" in week 3, I will first check... (hint: your error log — the errors will already be shrinking)
